lead: This unit teaches how to model a quantity that changes randomly with time, and how to predict its long-run behaviour. After it you can classify a random process, test stationarity, solve Markov chain limits, and compute autocorrelation and power spectra.
about: This unit moves from a random variable to a random signal. Chapter 7.1 defines a random process and sorts processes by time and state. Chapter 7.2 adds stationarity in strict and wide sense, and ergodicity. Chapter 7.3 treats Poisson and renewal counts as the standard arrival models. Chapter 7.4 introduces discrete-time Markov chains, transition matrices and state classes. Chapter 7.5 solves for limiting and steady-state distributions. Chapter 7.6 passes to continuous-time chains and generator matrices. Chapter 7.7 defines autocorrelation, cross-correlation and power spectral density. Chapter 7.8 sends random signals through LTI systems; only a few universities teach it. Chapter 7.9 closes with Gaussian processes and noise. Each chapter uses the earlier probability units, and the later chapters reuse the same two-state and Poisson examples.

chapters.idea: A random process is a rule that attaches a random variable to every time instant, so one experiment gives one whole sample path.
chapters.depth: Define {X(t): t in T} with index set T and state space S. A sample path (realization) is the observed function for one outcome. Classify by T discrete or continuous time, by S discrete or continuous state, and by dependence: independent, Markov, stationary. Some syllabi say stochastic process for random process, and sample function for sample path. Introduce ensemble versus time averages only as words; details come in 7.2.

figure.aria: A classification tree splits random processes by discrete or continuous time and by discrete or continuous state.

chapters.example: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly. Let X(n) be the number of heads after n tosses, with X(0)=0. (a) Give the index set T and state space S. (b) Write the sample path for tosses H, T, H. (c) Classify the process by time and state. Answer: T={0,1,2,...}, S={0,1,2,...}; path 0,1,1,2; discrete-time, discrete-state.
chapters.trap: Do not call the state space the set of time values; t is the index, X(t) is the state.
chapters.leave: Stationarity, Markov property details and distributions go to 7.2–7.6.

chapters.idea: Stationarity means the process's statistics do not depend on where the clock starts; ergodicity means one long record tells you those statistics.
chapters.depth: Strict-sense stationary: all finite-dimensional CDFs are unchanged by a time shift. Wide-sense stationary (WSS): mean μ_X is constant, variance finite, and autocovariance C_X(t1,t2) depends only on τ=t2−t1. Define autocorrelation R_X(τ)=E[X(t)X(t+τ)]. Give properties R_X(0)=E[X²], even, |R_X(τ)|≤R_X(0). Ergodicity in mean: time average over a long record tends to μ_X; ergodicity in autocorrelation similarly. Some syllabi write weakly stationary for WSS.

figure.aria: A cosine autocorrelation curve falls below zero and repeats with lag.

chapters.example: Let X(t)=2 cos(2πt+Θ), where Θ is uniform on [0,2π). Find μ_X, R_X(τ), variance. Is X WSS? Is its time average over a whole number of cycles equal to μ_X? Answer: μ_X=0, R_X(τ)=2cos(2πτ), variance=2; WSS; time average over integer cycles is 0.
chapters.trap: WSS does not require the distribution to be Gaussian or the process to be ergodic; strict stationarity with infinite variance need not be WSS.

chapters.idea: The Poisson process counts events that occur independently at a constant rate; a renewal process keeps the independent interarrival idea but allows any interarrival distribution.
chapters.depth: Poisson process {N(t), t≥0}: N(0)=0, independent increments, stationary increments, and P(N(t)=k)=e^{−λt}(λt)^k/k!, k=0,1,2,...; λ is the rate per unit time. Mean and variance both λt. Interarrival times are iid exponential with mean 1/λ; the k-th arrival time is gamma. Mention merging and thinning. Renewal process: interarrival times iid with mean μ; renewal function m(t)=E[N(t)]; elementary renewal theorem m(t)/t→1/μ. Some syllabi call the Poisson process a pure birth process.

figure.aria: A timeline shows three interarrival intervals of 2 hours, 4 hours and 1 hour, ending at 7 hours.

chapters.example: A help desk receives calls as a Poisson process with rate λ=0.5 per hour. (a) Find the probability of no call in 2 hours. (b) Find the mean and variance of the number of calls in 6 hours. (c) The first three interarrival times are 2 h, 4 h and 1 h; find the first three arrival times. Answer: (a) e^{−1}=0.3679; (b) mean 3, variance 3; (c) 2 h, 6 h, 7 h.
chapters.trap: For a Poisson count in an interval, use the interval length in the rate; mean and variance are equal, but do not use the exponential formula for the count.
chapters.leave: Markov chain jumps to 7.4; CTMC birth process to 7.6.

chapters.idea: A discrete-time Markov chain forgets the past once the present state is known; its one-step transition matrix P generates all multi-step probabilities.
chapters.depth: State space; Markov property P(X_{n+1}=j | X_n=i, past)=P_ij. Homogeneous transition matrix P=(P_ij), row sums 1. n-step transition P^(n)=P^n; Chapman–Kolmogorov. Classify states: communicate, irreducible, recurrent/transient, positive recurrent, periodic/aperiodic, absorbing. Some syllabi use transition probability matrix for P and ergodic for irreducible positive recurrent aperiodic. Compute P² for a two-state chain.

figure.aria: A two-state directed graph has self-loops and cross edges labelled with transition probabilities.

chapters.example: A weather chain has states S (sunny) and R (rainy) with P = [[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]], rows S,R. (a) Draw the state diagram. (b) Find P². (c) Classify the chain: irreducible? aperiodic? recurrent? Answer: P² = [[0.70,0.30],[0.45,0.55]]; irreducible, aperiodic, positive recurrent.
chapters.trap: Rows sum to 1, not columns; P² is matrix product P×P, not elementwise square.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 conditional probability; Unit 4 joint distributions; 7.1.
chapters.leave: Stationary limit to 7.5; continuous time to 7.6.

chapters.idea: A steady-state distribution is a probability vector π that the chain keeps unchanged; a limiting distribution is where the chain goes in the long run.
chapters.depth: Stationary distribution satisfies π=πP, Σπ_i=1, π_i≥0. For finite irreducible aperiodic chains it is unique and equals the limiting distribution. Periodic chains can have stationary π but no limit for some initial states. Mean recurrence time for state i is 1/π_i. Solve the linear system; for two states use one equation plus sum. Some syllabi call π the equilibrium or invariant distribution.

figure.aria: A plot of sunny probability against step number rises from 1 and settles towards 0.6.

chapters.example: For P = [[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]] (states S,R), start with p₀=(1,0). Find the stationary distribution π. Find p_n(S) and its limit. Find the mean recurrence time of S and R. Answer: π=(0.6,0.4); p_n(S)=0.6+0.4(0.5)^n; recurrence times 1.667 days and 2.5 days.
chapters.trap: A stationary distribution need not be the limiting distribution for a periodic chain; do not omit the sum-to-one equation.
chapters.leave: Ergodicity theory to 7.2; CTMC balance equations to 7.6.

chapters.idea: In continuous time the chain holds each state for an exponential sojourn, then jumps by a discrete chain; rates replace probabilities.
chapters.depth: Continuous-time Markov chain {X(t)}: Markov property; transition probabilities P_ij(t)=P(X(t)=j | X(0)=i). Generator Q=(q_ij): q_ij≥0 for i≠j, q_ii=−Σ_{j≠i}q_ij, row sums 0. Sojourn in state i is exponential with rate −q_ii, mean 1/(−q_ii). Jump chain uses p_ij=q_ij/(−q_ii). Kolmogorov forward/backward equations; stationary distribution solves πQ=0, Σπ=1. Birth–death process as example; Poisson process is a pure birth chain. Some syllabi call Q the infinitesimal generator or rate matrix; a Markov process is the general name, a CTMC is the countable-state case.

figure.aria: A two-state rate diagram shows a jump from state 0 to state 1 at rate 2 and back at rate 3.

chapters.example: A two-state CTMC has state 0→1 rate 2 per hour and state 1→0 rate 3 per hour. Write Q. Find the stationary distribution. Find the mean sojourn time in each state. Answer: Q = [[−2,2],[3,−3]], π=(0.6,0.4), sojourns 0.5 h and 0.333 h.
chapters.trap: Q row sums are zero, not one; the off-diagonal entries are rates, so they can exceed 1.
chapters.leave: Poisson count details to 7.3; spectral analysis to 7.7.

chapters.idea: Autocorrelation measures how a random signal relates to its shifted copy; its Fourier transform, the power spectral density, shows how power is spread over frequency.
chapters.depth: For WSS X(t): autocorrelation R_X(τ)=E[X(t)X(t+τ)], autocovariance C_X(τ)=R_X(τ)−μ_X². Cross-correlation R_XY(τ)=E[X(t)Y(t+τ)]. Properties: R_X(0)=E[X²], even, maximum at 0. Power spectral density S_X(ω)=∫R_X(τ)e^{−jωτ}dτ (Wiener–Khinchin). Total average power R_X(0)=(1/2π)∫S_X(ω)dω. Cross-PSD similarly. For a random vector, the autocorrelation matrix has entries E[X_i X_j]. Some syllabi use spectral density for PSD.

figure.aria: A power spectral density plot is a symmetric peak centred at zero frequency.

chapters.example: A zero-mean WSS process has R_X(τ)=4e^{−2|τ|}. Find the variance, the total average power, and the power spectral density S_X(ω). Answer: variance=4, power=4, S_X(ω)=16/(4+ω²).
chapters.trap: R_X(0) is power, not variance unless the mean is zero; the Fourier transform uses τ, not t.
chapters.leave: LTI filtering to 7.8; Gaussian noise spectra to 7.9.

chapters.idea: An LTI system cannot create new frequencies; it scales each frequency by |H(ω)|² and shifts the mean by H(0).
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. For a stable LTI system with impulse response h(t) and frequency response H(ω), a WSS input X(t) gives a WSS output Y(t). Mean μ_Y=H(0)μ_X. Output PSD S_Y(ω)=|H(ω)|²S_X(ω). Output autocorrelation R_Y(τ)=h(τ)*h(−τ)*R_X(τ) (double convolution). White noise through a filter. Keep derivations short.

figure.title: Random input through LTI
figure.aria: A block diagram passes a random input X(t) through an LTI system to produce a random output Y(t).

chapters.example: White noise with PSD S_X(ω)=2 passes through an RC low-pass filter with H(ω)=1/(1+j0.5ω). Find S_Y(ω) and the output average power. Answer: S_Y(ω)=2/(1+0.25ω²), average power=2.
chapters.trap: Use |H(ω)|², not H(ω); the output mean is H(0) times input mean, not always zero.
chapters.leave: Gaussian property to 7.9; circuit analysis outside scope.

chapters.idea: A Gaussian process is fixed completely by its mean and covariance; Gaussian noise is the standard model for random fluctuations.
chapters.depth: Gaussian process: every finite set X(t1),...,X(tn) has a multivariate normal distribution. For a Gaussian process, WSS implies strict stationarity. White Gaussian noise: zero mean, PSD constant N0/2, autocorrelation (N0/2)δ(τ), independent samples in continuous time (ideal model). Filtered Gaussian noise stays Gaussian. Thermal noise, receiver noise. Some syllabi call it normal process. Use Unit 4 multivariate normal.

figure.aria: A normal probability density curve is centred at 2 with spread set by standard deviation 3.

chapters.example: A Gaussian process X(t) has mean μ=2 and covariance C(τ)=9e^{−|τ|/2}. (a) Find P(X(0)≤5). (b) Find Var[X(3)−X(0)]. Answer: (a) 0.8413; (b) 18(1−e^{−1.5})=13.98.
chapters.trap: A process can have Gaussian marginal distributions but not be a Gaussian process; joint normality of all finite collections is required.
chapters.leave: Filtering formulas to 7.8; estimation to Unit 5.
